text: In the 1740s, electricity was a party trick. Traveling lecturers rubbed glass tubes with silk and made sparks fly from people's fingers and hair. Audiences paid to feel the shock. In Philadelphia, a printer called Benjamin Franklin saw one of these shows and could not stop thinking about it. He was so curious that he handed his printing business to a partner, so he would have time to study electricity. His most exciting tool was a new invention called a Leyden jar. It was a glass jar lined with metal foil, and it could store electricity, then let it all go at once in a bright spark with a loud crack. And that spark reminded Franklin of something, a flash of light, a crack of noise, a sharp smell in the air. It was like a tiny thunderstorm in a jar. So in November 1749, he wrote a list in his notebook, twelve ways a spark was just like lightning. They both gave light of the same color. They both moved in crooked lines. They both made a crack, set things on fire, and could kill animals. But a list of likenesses isn't proof. At the bottom of the page, Franklin wrote five famous words: "Let the experiment be made." But how do you catch a bolt of lightning without it killing you?
